title: What is the Image of God?
aliases: image of god in the bible
summary: Genesis connects the image of God with humanity's place in creation and responsibility for other living things. Later passages link image language with human dignity, speech, and renewal in Christ, so readers can follow the theme from creation into communal life and transformation.
historical_context: The cited passages develop the image theme through Scripture itself: Genesis 1 connects it with humanity's role in creation, Genesis 5 repeats the language across generations, and Genesis 9 invokes it when addressing the taking of human life. Psalm 8 reflects on human responsibility, while Colossians 3 and Romans 8 speak of renewal and conformity to Christ's image. This textual sequence does not depend on a comparison with royal titles in other cultures.
canonical_context: The references show several dimensions of image language. Genesis 1:26–28 places it alongside humanity's responsibility for other creatures; Genesis 5:1–3 carries the image and likeness language into the next generation; and Genesis 9:6 invokes it as a reason human life matters. James 3:9 applies related likeness language to the way people speak about one another. Colossians 3:9–10 and Romans 8:29 then describe renewal and conformity to the image of the Son. The connections broaden the theme without requiring one sentence to settle every question about what the image is.
literary_context: Watch how each passage uses the language. Genesis 1 places image and likeness beside blessing and the task of ruling over other creatures; Genesis 5 repeats the terms in its genealogy; Genesis 9 uses image language in a prohibition against bloodshed. Psalm 8 is a poem about humanity's place in creation, while James 3 turns likeness language toward the ethics of speech. Colossians 3 and Romans 8 use image language for renewal and becoming like the Son.
covenantal_significance: Genesis 9:6 connects the image of God with the seriousness of taking human life, and James 3:9 draws on humanity's likeness to God when warning against cursing other people. These passages make the theme ethically consequential: how people treat and speak about other humans matters. Colossians 3:9–10 adds that renewed life is described in terms of the image of the creator.
canonical_role: What is the Image of God? serves as a question-oriented anchor, connecting common reader language to related passages, themes, and CKL entries.

interpretive_notes.note: Genesis 1:26–28 places image language alongside responsibility for other creatures; Genesis 9:6 connects it with the value of human life. These passages support a representational and ethical dimension without reducing the image to one physical feature.

Colossians 3:9–10 speaks of renewal in the creator's image, and Romans 8:29 of being conformed to the Son's image. These texts support a theme of renewal, but Genesis 1 itself does not use the later wording about the image being distorted by sin.
